```{r load_emergence, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
emergence <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/fry_emergence.csv")
emergence$yday <- yday(emergence$date)

emergence$time_set_numeric <- with(emergence, {
  hours <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 1, 2))
  minutes <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 4, 5)) / 60
  adjusted_hours <- ifelse(hours < 10, hours + 24, hours)  # Add 24 if after midnight
  (adjusted_hours + minutes) - 20
})

emergence <- emergence %>% mutate(volume_m3 = ifelse(volume_m3<0, NA, volume_m3),
                                  mean_nightly_discharge_cms = ifelse(mean_nightly_discharge_cms>100, NA, mean_nightly_discharge_cms)) %>% 
  mutate(total_catch = as.integer(total_catch))

new_moons <- data.frame()
for(i in 1:length(unique(emergence$sample_year))){
  year <- unique(emergence$sample_year)[i]
  start_date <- as.Date(paste(year,"-04-06", sep = ""))
  dates <- seq(start_date, start_date+29, by = "day")
  new_moons <- bind_rows(new_moons, data.frame(year = year, new_moon_date = dates[which.min(lunar.illumination(dates))], new_moon_yday = yday(dates[which.min(lunar.illumination(dates))])))
}

emergence <- emergence %>% left_join(new_moons %>% rename(sample_year = year))

emergence_select <- emergence %>% select(date, brood_year, sample_year, total_catch, soak_time_min, yday, time_set_numeric, volume_m3) %>% 
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>% 
  filter(time_set_numeric >= 0, time_set_numeric<=5) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(total_catch)) |> 
  filter(soak_time_min >=5, soak_time_min<=20)
```


```{r dusk, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
dusk <- getSunlightTimes(date = emergence_select$date, lat = 49.1823, lon = -119.5504, keep = "dusk", tz = "Etc/GMT+7")

dusk <- dusk %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>%
  mutate(dusk_hour = hour(dusk) + minute(dusk)/60)

ggplot(dusk, aes(x = yday, y = dusk_hour))+
  geom_point()

emergence_select$dusk <- dusk$dusk_hour

ggplot(emergence_select, aes(x = yday, y = dusk))+
  geom_point()
```

```{r thermal_units, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
temperature <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/ok_river_mean_daily_temperatures.csv")
#tabyl(temperature, location)
temperature$date <- as.Date(temperature$date)

temperature2 <- read.csv("../../ok_watertemp/data/oliver_air_water_temp_data.csv")
temperature2$date <- as.Date(temperature2$date)

temperature <- temperature %>% 
  select(date, temp = water_temperature_c, location) %>% 
  bind_rows(temperature2 %>% select(date, temp = mean_water_temp) %>% mutate(location = "Oliver2"))

# ggplot(temperature, aes(x = yday(date), y = temp))+
#   geom_line(aes(color = location))+
#   facet_wrap(~year(date))

temp_means <- temperature %>% 
  filter(!(location == "Okanagan River near Oliver, BC" & date >= as.Date("2007-06-01") & date <= as.Date("2008-05-30"))) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  summarise(temperature = mean(temp,na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(temp_means, aes(x = yday(date), y = temperature))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(100, 319))+
  geom_line()+
  facet_wrap(~year(date))

incubation_start_full <- as.Date("2025-10-15")
incubation_end_full <- as.Date("2025-04-10")

incubation_start <- format(incubation_start_full, "%B ") %>%
  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_start_full, "%d")))

ATU.df <- temp_means %>% 
  mutate(year_start = if_else(format(date, "%m-%d") >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d"),
                              year(date),
                              year(date) - 1)) %>% 
  group_by(year_start) %>% 
  arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(ATU = cumsum(temperature)) %>% 
  ungroup()

ggplot(ATU.df, aes(x = yday(date), y = ATU, color = factor(year_start)))+
  geom_path()

ATU_day100 <- ATU.df %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>% 
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  filter(yday == yday(incubation_end_full))

ATU_day700 <- ATU.df %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>% 
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  filter(ATU<700, ATU>650) %>% 
  group_by(year) %>% 
  filter(ATU == max(ATU))

env.df <- new_moons %>% 
  left_join(ATU_day100 %>% select(year, ATU))

ggplot(env.df, aes(x = new_moon_yday, y = ATU))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year))

summary(lm(ATU ~ new_moon_yday, data = env.df))
```

```{r flow, include=FALSE}
flow <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/ok_river_mean_daily_flows.csv") %>% 
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), yday = yday(date), year = year(date)) %>% 
  mutate(month_day = format(date, "%m-%d")) %>% 
  group_by(month_day) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage = first(life_stage)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage2 = ifelse(month_day >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d") | month_day <= format(incubation_end_full, "%m-%d"), "incubation", life_stage)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage = factor(life_stage, levels = c("incubation", "fry migration", "rearing", "adult migration", "spawn"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage2 = factor(life_stage2, levels = c("incubation", "fry migration", "rearing", "adult migration", "spawn"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  filter(brood_year >= min(emergence$brood_year)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(5, 28.3), lty = 2)+
  geom_point(size = 0.1)+
  facet_wrap(~life_stage2)+
  ylab("flow rate m3/s")+
  xlab("")+
  scale_color_discrete(guide = "none")+
  scale_y_log10()

scour_des <- flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  mutate(scour = max(c(value - 28.5, 0)), desiccation = max(c(5 - value, 0))) %>% 
  ungroup()

scour_des_sum <- scour_des %>% 
  group_by(brood_year, life_stage2) %>% 
  summarise(non_range_days = sum(scour > 0) + sum(desiccation>0),
            total_scour = sum(scour), 
            total_desiccation = sum(desiccation), 
            flow_mean = mean(value), 
            flow_max = max(value), 
            flow_min = min(value), 
            flow_median = median(value), n = n()) %>% 
  group_by(life_stage2) %>% 
  mutate(max_n = max(n)) %>% 
  filter(n > max_n-2) %>% 
  select(-n, -max_n) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(year = brood_year + 1)

env.df <- env.df %>% left_join(scour_des_sum %>% filter(life_stage2 == "incubation") %>% select(year, non_range_days, total_scour, total_desiccation))
```

```{r stan, include = FALSE}
dayV <- seq(min(emergence_select$yday)-3, max(emergence_select$yday)+5)


dat_list <- list(Y = length(unique(emergence_select$sample_year)),
                 N = nrow(emergence_select),
                 D = length(dayV),
                 year = as.numeric(factor(emergence_select$sample_year)),
                 fry_obs = emergence_select$total_catch,
                 soak_time = stand(emergence_select$soak_time_min),
                 day = emergence_select$yday - min(emergence_select$yday) + 1,
                 hour = stand(emergence_select$time_set_numeric),
                 new_moon_date = stand(env.df$new_moon_yday),
                 ATU = stand(env.df$ATU),
                 dusk = stand(emergence_select$dusk), 
                 exceeded_FWMT = as.numeric(env.df$non_range_days>0),
                 testalinden = ifelse(env.df$year == 2011, 1, 0),
                 day_std = (dayV - mean(emergence_select$yday))/sd(emergence_select$yday),
                 spawner_ln_est = env.df$spawners_ln_est,
                 spawner_ln_sd = env.df$spawner_ln_sd,
                 
                 sigma_sf_prior = 1,
                 beta_sf_prior = 1,
                 alpha_sf_prior = -3,
                 beta_sf_sigma_prior = 1,
                 alpha_sf_sigma_prior = 1
)

init_year <- min(emergence_select$sample_year) - 1

stan_file <- "../code/stan/emergence.stan"
fit <- run_or_load_model(
  model_name = "emerge_m",
  stan_path = stan_file,
  data_list = dat_list, 
  cache_dir = "../model_fits",
  chains = 4, 
  threads_per_chain = 1,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  seed = 123
)
```

```{r fryemerge, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
total_fry_ln <- spread_draws(fit, total_fry_ln[year]) |>

  group_by(brood_year, emergence_year) |> 
  summarise(median = median(total_fry_ln), sd = sd(total_fry_ln))

total_fry.df <- spread_draws(fit, total_fry_ln[year]) |> 
  mutate(emergence_year = year + init_year) |> 
  mutate(brood_year = emergence_year - 1) |>
  group_by(brood_year, emergence_year) |> 
  summarise(total_fry = median(exp(total_fry_ln)))

fig_fry_emerge_cap <- paste0("Estimated fry emergence timing and relative abundance and factors influencing emergence timing. Panel A shows the estimated emergence relative abundance across dates where each line represents a single year. Panel B shows the estimated coefficients for the effect of the timing of dusk (dusk), the date of first new moon after ", sub("^0", "", format(start_date, "%B %d")), " (moon), the accumulated thermal units (ATU) since ", incubation_start, ", and the interaction between new moon date and ATUs (moon x ATU) on emergence timing. Panels C and D show the relationships between the date of the new moon (C) or the accumulated thermal units (D) and the estimated peak emergence date across years. The dashed line in panel C shows the 1:1 relationship between the date of the new moon and the estimated peak fry emergence date. The colours in panels A, C, and D show the 5 year period each year falls within. Points and error bars in panels B--D show the posterior medians with 66% and 95% credible intervals.")
```

```{r spawner_fry, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
spawnV <- seq(0, exp(max(env.df$spawners_ln_est, na.rm = TRUE)), length = 30)

FWMT_BH.df <- data.frame()
for(j in 0:1){
  alpha_sf <- exp(post$alpha0 + post$a_FWMT * j)
  for(i in 1:length(spawnV)){
    total_fry = (alpha_sf * spawnV[i])/(1 + post$beta_sf * (spawnV[i]/1e05) ^ post$theta_sf)
    #mu = log((alpha_sf * spawnV[i])/(1 + post$beta_sf * spawnV[i]/1e05));
    #total_fry <-exp(rnorm(length(post$beta_sf), mu, post$sigma_sf))
    FWMT_BH.df <- bind_rows(FWMT_BH.df, data.frame(spawners = spawnV[i], FWMT_range = c("within", "outside")[j+1], total_fry = total_fry, draw = 1:length(post$beta_sf)))
  }
}

FWMT_BH_summary.df<- FWMT_BH.df %>% 
  group_by(spawners, FWMT_range) %>% 
  summarise(l95 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.025), 
            u95 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.975),
            l66 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.165), 
            u66 = quantile(total_fry, probs = 0.835),
            total_fry = median(total_fry))

alpha_sf <- exp(post$alpha0 + post$a_FWMT * 0)
mu_FWMT <-(alpha_sf * spawnV[i])/(1 + post$beta_sf * (spawnV[i]/1e05)^ post$theta_sf);
alpha_sf <- exp(post$alpha0 + post$a_FWMT * 1)
mu_noFWMT <-(alpha_sf * spawnV[i])/(1 + post$beta_sf * (spawnV[i]/1e05)^ post$theta_sf);

alpha_sf <- exp(post$alpha0 + post$sf_ATU * min(dat_list$ATU))
mu_lowATU <-(alpha_sf * spawnV[i])/(1 + post$beta_sf * (spawnV[i]/1e05)^ post$theta_sf);
alpha_sf <- exp(post$alpha0 + post$sf_ATU * max(dat_list$ATU))
mu_highATU <-(alpha_sf * spawnV[i])/(1 + post$beta_sf * (spawnV[i]/1e05)^ post$theta_sf);

fry_percent_change <- data.frame(draw = 1:length(mu_FWMT), FWMT = 100 * (mu_FWMT - mu_noFWMT)/mu_noFWMT, ATU = 100 * (mu_highATU - mu_lowATU)/mu_lowATU)

env_post$fry_abund_predict <- total_fry.df$total_fry

p1 <- ggplot(FWMT_BH_summary.df, aes(x = spawners, y = total_fry, color = FWMT_range, fill = FWMT_range, group = FWMT_range))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = l95, ymax = u95), alpha =0.2, color = NA)+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point(data = env_post %>% mutate(FWMT_range = ifelse(non_range_days == 0, "within", "outside")), aes(y = fry_abund_predict))+
  stat_pointinterval(data = spread_draws(fit, total_fry_ln[year]) %>% 
                       mutate(year = init_year + year) %>% 
                       left_join(env_post %>% 
                                   mutate(FWMT_range = ifelse(non_range_days == 0, "within", "outside")) %>% 
                                   select(year, FWMT_range, spawners)) %>% 
                       mutate(total_fry = exp(total_fry_ln)), 
                     .width = CIs)+
  geom_text_repel(
    data = env_post %>% mutate(FWMT_range = ifelse(non_range_days == 0, "within", "outside")),
    aes(y = fry_abund_predict, label = brood_year),
    nudge_x = -10000,           # consistent rightward offset
    direction = "y",           # only allow vertical movement
    box.padding = 0.2,         # optional fine-tuning
    min.segment.length = 0,    # ensures connecting lines are drawn
    segment.alpha = 0.5,
    size = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  )+
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "black"), "FWMT range")+
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "black"), "FWMT range")+
  ylab("Fry abundance (relative)")+
  theme(legend.position = c(0.05, 0.95), legend.justification = c(0, 1))+
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"), name = "Spawner abundance (thousands)")

p3 <- fry_percent_change %>%
  gather(key = variable, value = percent_change, -draw) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = percent_change))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2)+
  stat_pointinterval(.width = CIs)+
  ylab("% change in fry production")+
  xlab("")+
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(
    "ATU" = "High\nATUs",
    "FWMT" = "FWMT\ncompliant"
  ))

fig_spawn_fry_cap <- paste0("Estimated spawner to emerging fry abundance relationship (A) comparing scenarios where flows are maintained within the FWMT range (5–28.5 m\u00B3/s; black), or not (red), for the entire incubation period (", format(incubation_start_full, "%B ") %>%  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_start_full, "%d"))),"–", format(incubation_end_full, "%B ") %>%  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_end_full, "%d"))),"). Panel B shows the estimated percent change in fry due to maintaining flows within the FWMT range, and between the highest (", round(max(env.df$ATU)), "°C·d) vs. lowest (",round(min(env.df$ATU)),"°C·d) observed accumulated thermal units during the incubation period. The lines and shaded areas in panel A show the median and the 95% credible intervals of the mean spawner–fry relationships under each flow scenario, assuming average ATUs. Points and error bars in both panels show the posterior medians with 66% and 95% credible intervals for year-specific estimates (A) and effect sizes (B). Year is spawning year/brood year.")
```
# Abstract
Maintaining flows during the incubation-period within the target range from the Fish Water Management Tools $(5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s})$ is estimated to increase fry abundance by `r round(median(fry_percent_change$FWMT))`% (95% CI:`r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT, 0.025))`--`r round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT, 0.975))`%) with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$FWMT>0)*100)`% probability that the effect is positive.

# Introduction
Sockeye salmon *Oncorhynchus nerka* populations are in decline over much of their southern range in North America [@rand2012; @grant2019], highlighting the urgent need for management measures that can boost survival and contribute to maintenance and recovery. In this context, the Okanagan sockeye represent a rare success story where targeted management measures have proven effective [@alexander2024], resulting in a twenty fold increase in spawner abundance since the early 2000s [@bailey2025]. However, because multiple management measures were implemented concurrently---habitat restoration, a hatchery restocking program, improved dam passage, managing dam outflows to ensure "fish-friendly flows"---and corresponded with changing environmental conditions, it has proven challenging to quantify the contribution of each intervention. Based on a weight of evidence approach, @alexander2024 concluded that these management interventions jointly contributed to the recovery, and amplified the positive effects of a 2007 shift towards more favourable coastal marine conditions. Still, quantitative estimates of how individual management interventions impact productivity and survival are needed in order to ensure that limited conservation resources are used effectively, and to assess whether similar intervention could support recovery in other salmon populations. 

This study focuses on one of these interventions: the regulation of dam flows in the Okanagan River to maintain suitable conditions during egg incubation, reducing the risk of scouring from high flows and desiccation from low flows. Sockeye salmon spawn in autumn when they lay their eggs in pockets (i.e., redds) in the gravel of streams, and these eggs incubate over the winter, hatching into alevins, before emerging as fry in the spring [@wilson2025]. During this period, high flows can scour the stream bed, potentially dislodging or burying eggs and alevin, while also increasing fine sediment infiltration, which in turn reduces oxygen supply [@devries1997; @ingram2011]. The degree to which scour reduces survival is assumed to be a sigmoidal function of the depth reached by scour, which increases with flow velocity [@glawdel2011]. Sockeye redds tend to be buried at depths between 10 and 25 cm below the stream bed [@devries1997] and survival is determined by the proportion of the eggs that are impacted by scour. Likewise, if flows are low enough to expose the eggs to air, mortality can occur through desiccation or freezing [@casas-mulet2015]. 

While scouring flows during the incubation period can reduce survival, they may have beneficial effects if they occur at other times of year. Over time, fine sediments can accumulate in spawning habitat, filling the spaces between spawning gravels, and causing mortality by reducing dissolved oxygen and trapping emerging alevins [@moring1982]. High-velocity flows, such as those during freshet, can flush fine sediments from spawning gravel, and may be critical to maintaining productive spawning habitat [@reiser1989].

While desiccation, scour, and sediment flushing occur naturally, they are directly influenced by dam-influenced flow regulation, as is the case in the Okanagan River. Because of this, the Okanagan Basin Implementation Board adopted seasonally varying target flows in 1976, to ensure that flow is suitable for each life stage of salmon in the river [@okanaganbasinimplementationboard1982], but challenges associated with balancing flood mitigation as well as uncertainty in real-time conditions resulted in flows frequently exceeding or falling below this range [@ng2025]. To address this issue, the Fish/Water Management Tool (FWMT) was developed as a decision support tool that provides real-time predictions of the consequences of water management decisions for fish and other users [@hyatt2015]. Since its implementation in 2004, there have been fewer days where flows fell below or exceeded the target flow range [@ng2025; @alexander2024]. 

It has been assumed that improved flow compliance has reduced scour and desiccation, and thus improved egg to fry survival; however, quantifying this benefit is challenging due to limited fry abundance data prior to FWMT implementation. @ng2025 found that emerging fry recruitment (i.e., fry per spawner) was higher in the 19 years after the FWMT was implemented, compared to the three years prior. Similarly, @alexander2024 found a two-fold increase in the ratio of pre-smolts (i.e., in-lake fry in the fall and winter following emergence) to spawners after brood year 2008 (four years post FWMT implementation) and concluded that FWMT was a strong contributing factor to the sockeye recovery. However, despite this, neither study was able to establish a causal link between fry recruitment and interannual variation in flow rates.

<!-- Add review of temperature effects Beacham et al. 1990-->

Here we present a process-based Bayesian model that estimates how flow velocity and temperature, during and preceding the incubation period, influences spawner-to-fry production in the Okanagan River. This model allows us to test two hypotheses: 1) that higher pre-spawning flows improve spawner-to-fry production by flushing fine sediments, and 2) that high flows during incubation reduce production through scour-related mortality. While desiccation remains a potential concern, we were unable to estimate the effects of low flows, as flows remained above the assumed desiccation threshold during incubation in all but two years in our study period. By quantifying the benefits of managing for "fish-friendly" flows, this work supports the continued application of the FWMT and provides insight into how this approach could support the sustainable management of other salmon populations. 


# Methods 
## Study system
## Fry emergence sampling
The ONA has conducted fry emergence surveys in March and April of each year since `r min(emergence_select$sample_year)` (note: Elizabeth's report says surveys started in 2001). Sampling occurs roughly once per week starting in early March to capture the beginning of the emergence period, then switches to every three or four days once emerging fry abundance begins to increase, and decreases to every five to eight days once peak emergence is over. 

Emerging fry are sampled using a fyke net (dimensions?) deployed in the Okanagan River at Vertical Drop Structure 13 (Figure \ref{fig:map}). Sampling typically consists of four sets, starting on the hour between 21:00 and midnight, each with a 15-minute soak time. When issues arise due to debris accumulation, exceptionally high fish abundance, or flow, soak times are often reduced, but more sets are deployed, with the goal of obtaining a total soak time of one hour across all sets. Even so, there is additional variation in soak time and set timing, particularly in early years. Therefore, our analysis only includes sets with soak times between 5 and 20 minutes that occurred between 8 PM and 1 AM. This includes `r nrow(emergence_select)` sets over `r length(unique(emergence_select$date))` days, spanning `r length(unique(emergence_select$sample_year))` years from `r min(emergence_select$sample_year)` to `r max(emergence_select$sample_year)`. The total number of fry captured in each set is recorded, and since 2008, a flow meter has been used to estimate the volume of water sampled. 

## Estimating a metric of yearly fry abundance
The goal of these surveys is to estimate the peak and end dates of emergence. However, they can also provide a relative index of total fry abundance in each year. To estimate this index, we model the number of fry emerging each day as a latent (i.e., unobserved) process that varies across years. This daily emergence is linked to the observed fry counts from the individual sets, while controlling for variation in soak time, flow rate, sampling date, and time of day. To specify the latent emergence process, we assume that fry emerge over a range of days, with daily abundance following a normal distribution. Within each day, we assume that fry emergence follows a second normal distribution, peaking in the evening. The total number of fry, as well as the timing and spread of their emergence, vary across years such that:

$$\hat{N}_{y,d,h}^{\text{fry}} = \frac{\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}}{2\pi \cdot d_y^{\text{sd}} \cdot h_y^{\text{sd}}} \cdot 
\exp\left( 
- \frac{(d - d_y^{\text{peak}})^2}{2(d_y^{\text{sd}})^2} 
- \frac{(h - h_{y,d}^{\text{peak}})^2}{2(h_y^{\text{sd}})^2} 
\right),$$


where $\hat{N}_{y,d,h}^{\text{fry}}$ is fry abundance in year $y$ on day $d$ at hour $h$ and $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$ is the relative index of total fry abundance. Here, $d$ is day-of-year standardized so that $d = 1$ is the first survey date across all years, and $h$ is the standardized hour of the day ($\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$). The parameters $d_y^{\text{peak}}$ and $h_y^{\text{peak}}$ represent the peak day and hour of emergence, respectively, while $d_y^{\text{sd}}$ and $h_y^{\text{sd}}$ represent the spread of emergence across days and hours.

The timing of emergence has been shown to depend on the cumulative exposure of the eggs to temperature [@beacham1990]. In addition, Syilx traditional knowledge indicates that fry emergence is timed with the new moon---when moonlight is minimal---to reduce predation risk from visually oriented predators. It is therefore plausible that the effect of accumulated thermal units (ATU) and the date of the new moon may interactively influence emergence, such that fry may track the new moon date, but only when sufficient development has occurred. Thus, we modelled the annual timing of peak emergence, $d_y^{\text{peak}}$, as a normal distribution with a mean that varies by year according to standardized ($\mu$ = 0, $\sigma$ = 1) accumulated thermal units ($\text{ATU}_y$) and the date of the new moon ($\text{moon}_y$), defined as the first new moon following April 6, to align with the typical emergence period. This model includes a multiyear intercept $\mu_d^{\text{peak}}$ and a standard deviation $\sigma_d^{\text{peak}}$, which give it hierarchical structure across years: 

$$d_y^{\text{peak}} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_d^{\text{peak}} + \beta_d^{\text{ATU}} \cdot \text{ATU}_y + \beta_d^{\text{moon}} \cdot \text{moon}_y + \beta_d^{\text{ATU x moon}} \cdot (\text{ATU}_y \cdot \text{moon}_y), \sigma_d^{\text{peak}}).$$

The coefficients $\beta_d^{\text{ATU}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{moon}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{ATU x moon}}$ are the slopes describing the effect of accumulated thermal units, lunar timing, and their interaction, respectively, on peak emergence date. We used weakly regularizing, non-informative priors for $\mu_d^{\text{peak}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{ATU}}$, $\beta_d^{\text{moon}}$, and $\beta_d^{\text{ATU x moon}}$, each specified as $\text{Normal}(0, 0.5)$. The standard deviation parameter $\sigma_d^{\text{peak}}$ was assigned an $\text{Exponential}(1)$ prior to regularize interannual variation in peak emergence timing. 

Observations from the survey crew suggest that emergence timing within each day may be linked to the timing of dusk. Thus, we modelled daily peak emergence, $h_{y,d}^{\text{peak}}$, as a normal distribution with a mean that varies with the timing of dusk $\text{dusk}_{y,d}$, along with as on a hierarchical multiyear mean $\mu_{h}^{\text{peak}}$ and standard deviation, $\sigma_{h}^{\text{peak}}$:

$$h_{y,d}^{\text{peak}} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{h}^{\text{peak}} + \beta_{h}^{\text{dusk}} \cdot \text{dusk}_{y,d}, \sigma_{h}^{\text{peak}}).$$
We set the prior for $\mu_{h}^{\text{peak}}$ as $\text{Normal}(0, 0.5)$ to reflect the expectation that emergence peaks midway through the nightly sampling window. We used an $\text{Exponential}(10)$ for $\sigma_{h}^{\text{peak}}$, reflecting our expectation that nightly emergence timing not explained by dusk is likely small.


We modelled $d_y^{\text{sd}}$ and $h_y^{\text{sd}}$ hierarchically on a log scale (to enforce positivity), with yearly values drawn from a normal distribution defined by a multiyear mean and standard deviation. We set the priors for the the multiyear means to be $\text{Normal}(-0.5, 0.5)$ to reflect our expectation that the spread of emergence across both days and hours is relatively narrow. We set the priors for the standard deviations of the year-specific effects as $\text{Exponential}(10)$ as a weakly regularizing prior of variation on a log scale. 



### Process model for fry abundance in year y in day d.  
\begin{equation} \label{fry_abund_eq}
\begin{aligned}
\hat{N}_{y, d}^{\text{fry}} &= \hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}{}_{\text{max}} \cdot \exp\left( - \frac{(d - d_y^{\text{peak}})^2}{2(d_y^{\text{sd}})^2} \right)\\
\log \hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}{}_{\text{max}} &= \log N_y^{\text{fry}} - \log( 2\pi \cdot d_y^{\text{sd}} \cdot h_y^{\text{sd}} )\\
d_y^{\text{peak}} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_d^{\text{peak}} + \beta^{\text{moon}} \cdot \text{moon}_y + \beta_d^{\text{ATU}} \cdot \text{ATU}_y + \beta^{\text{moonxATU}} \cdot (\text{moon}_y \cdot \text{ATU}_y), \sigma_d^{\text{peak}})\\
\mu_d^{\text{peak}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)\\
\sigma_d^{\text{peak}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(1)\\
\log d_y^{\text{sd}} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_d^{\text{sd}}, \sigma_d^{\text{sd}})\\
\mu_d^{\text{sd}} &\sim \text{Normal}(-0.5, 0.5)\\
\sigma_d^{\text{sd}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(1)\\
\log h^{\text{sd}}_y &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_h^{\text{sd}}, \sigma_h^{\text{sd}})\\
\mu_h^{\text{sd}} &\sim \text{Normal}(-0.5, 0.5)\\
\sigma_h^{\text{sd}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(10)\\
\beta^{\text{moon}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)\\
\beta^{\text{ATU}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)\\
\beta^{\text{moonxATU}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)\\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

<!--We assume that fry emerge in the spring over a period of days following a Gaussian distribution such that emerging abundance peaks mid-way through their emergence.-->

### Spawner fry Beverton holt model
\begin{equation} \label{spawner_fry_eq}
\begin{aligned}
\log N_y^{\text{fry}} &\sim \text{Normal}(\log \mu_y^{sf}, \sigma_{\text{proc}}^{sf})\\
\mu_y^{sf} &= \frac{\alpha_y^{sf} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}}{1 + (\beta^{sf} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}/10^5)^{\Theta^{sf}}}\\
\log \alpha_y^{sf} &= \alpha_0^{sf} + \beta^{\text{FWMT}} \cdot \text{FWMT}_y + \beta^{\text{ATU}} \cdot \text{ATU}_y\\ 
\beta^{sf} &\sim \text{Lognormal}(1, 1)\\
\Theta^{sf} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)\\
\alpha_0^{sf} &\sim \text{Normal}(-3, 1)\\
\beta^{\text{FWMT}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)\\
\beta^{\text{ATU}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)\\
\sigma_{\text{proc}}^{sf} &\sim \text{Exponential}(1)\\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

### Observation model for emergence data  
\begin{equation} \label{emerge_obs_eq}
\begin{aligned}
N_i^{\text{fry}}{}_{\text{obs}} &\sim \text{NegativeBinomial}(\mu^{\text{fry}}_i, 1/\phi^{\text{fry}}) \\
\mu^{\text{fry}}_i &= \exp\left( \log \hat{N}_{y_i, d_i}^{\text{fry}} - \frac{(h_i - h_i^{\text{peak}})^2}{2 (h^{\text{sd}}_{y_i})^2} + \beta^{\text{soak}} \cdot t^{\text{soak}}_i \right) \\
h_i^{\text{peak}} &= \mu_{h, y_i}^{\text{peak}} + \beta^{\text{dusk}} \cdot \text{dusk}_i\\
\mu_{h, y}^{\text{peak}} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_h^{\text{peak}}, \sigma_h^{\text{peak}})\\
\mu_h^{\text{peak}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)\\
\sigma_h^{\text{peak}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(10)\\
\beta^{\text{soak}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\beta^{\text{dusk}} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5) \\
\phi^{\text{fry}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
